domain: Classical Javanese batik tulis wax-resist dyeing
axioms: Wax-resist work specifies an image negatively as well as positively: every applied boundary states where the next dye must not penetrate.
A small discontinuity in a reserve can remain inconspicuous before immersion yet permanently contaminate a protected region during the dye bath.
In multi-color work, wax application, dyeing, and wax removal form an ordered sequence; the same operation at a different stage does not produce the same cloth.
Inspection is most valuable while the relevant layer and its repair opportunity still exist; final reveal can expose a defect after its local cause has become ambiguous or irreversible.
Repeating a stage is not restoration: once dye crosses a reserve, another application of wax cannot recover the original undyed ground.

Indonesian batik achieves selective color by drawing hot-wax reserves, dyeing the cloth, removing wax with boiling water, and repeating the process for multiple colors ([UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage](https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/indonesian-batik-00170)).
failure_mode: The lens may overstate irreversibility because source-control changes are often cheaply reversible, although generated artifacts, external effects, and lost diagnostic state may not be.
It can encourage excessive intermediate gates that erase the token and latency gains Pattern F is meant to obtain.
Negative reserves can grow into an unbounded catalogue of prohibitions, recreating main-thread context inside every plan unless the design finds a compact, reusable representation.
Visual boundary leakage has a spatial clarity that semantic software side effects often lack, so the mapping may make protected surfaces seem easier to enumerate than they are.
